standard.title: Causes and Effects of European Contact on an Asian Society
standard.description: the causes and effects of European contact, including colonialisation, on an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have established an understanding of the selected Asian society's features before European contact (AC9HH9K19). They understand what the society was like before external pressure intensified. This descriptor asks them to examine what changed — the causes of European contact and its effects on the selected society.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine the causes and effects of European contact including colonisation on one Asian society, identifying what changed and what remained.

nodes.label: Causes of European contact and colonial interest
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the causes of European contact with the selected Asian society, including commercial, strategic, and imperial motivations.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two causes of European contact with the selected Asian society.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the causes of European contact including: commercial interests (trade, raw materials, markets); strategic competition between European powers; missionary and civilising ideology; for China — the British opium trade as a deliberate strategy to address trade imbalance; for India — the role of the British East India Company as a commercial actor that became a political power; for Indonesia — Dutch colonial commercial interests from the 17th century.
wider: Examine the British opium trade as a deliberate commercial and political strategy — analysing how Britain deliberately created addiction in China to resolve a trade deficit, and assess how this represents a specific form of colonial economic coercion
Investigate how the East India Company transitioned from a trading company to a governing colonial authority — tracing the stages by which commercial interests became territorial control

Compare the colonial motivations and methods of two European powers operating in Asia (e.g. British in India vs Dutch in Indonesia) to assess whether there were common or distinctive colonial approaches
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that European contact was driven by specific interests (commercial, strategic, ideological) — not by inevitability or benevolence — is essential for analysing effects. Without this, students cannot explain why contact took the particular forms it did or why it produced the effects it did.

response_modes.reason: Students need an explicit framework for understanding colonial motivation — not just listing 'trade and religion' but explaining how commercial interests created political pressure that eventually produced colonial domination. The East India Company trajectory is a particularly useful model.

success_criteria: Describes at least two causes of European contact with the selected Asian society, drawing on historical evidence
Explains how at least one cause (commercial, strategic, or ideological) shaped the nature of European engagement

nodes.label: Effects of European contact — change and continuity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify aspects of the selected Asian society that changed and aspects that remained as a result of European contact, explaining the nature and significance of key effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two effects of European contact on the selected Asian society — one change and one continuity.
nodes.typical_width: Identify aspects of the selected Asian society that changed and remained during this period; describe the reasons for and effects of European contact including: for China — effects of the opium trade, the Opium Wars, and the unequal treaties; for India — the development of the British Raj, British influences (roads, railways, education, law) and their costs; for Indonesia — the short- and long-term effects of Dutch trade and colonisation from the 17th century.
wider: Examine the 'dual economy' of colonial India — where British infrastructure investment (railways, telegraph) served colonial extraction rather than Indian development — to assess how 'modernisation' under colonialism was structured to benefit the coloniser
Investigate the effects of European contact on traditional cultural and religious practices in the selected society — examining what was destroyed, suppressed, or adapted under colonial pressure
Compare the immediate and long-term effects of European contact on one Asian society — examining what changed quickly and what proved resilient over decades of colonial presence

response_modes.reason: The change/continuity framework is the core analytical tool here. Using both — what changed AND what remained — is important to avoid a complete-disruption narrative that denies the resilience and continuity of Asian societies under colonial pressure.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The effects of colonialism on Asian societies are pedagogically rich because they complicate simple narratives (either 'colonialism was totally destructive' or 'colonialism brought progress') — the reality of selective change and persistent continuity is more historically accurate and more intellectually demanding.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two effects of European contact on the selected Asian society, including both changes and continuities
Explains at least one effect with reference to specific historical evidence (an event, a policy, or a primary source)
